newsitem.title: USA: U.S. gives car-makers OK to reduce airbag power.
newsitem.headline: U.S. gives car-makers OK to reduce airbag power.

text.p: The federal government said Friday it will allow automakers to install lower-powered air bags in cars and trucks starting this summer in a bid to save lives.
But the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) delayed a final decision on its controversial proposal to allow consumers to disconnect their air bags if they feel unsafe.
Deputy NHTSA Administrator Philip Recht said the agency is still weighing the disconnection issue but declined to offer a timetable for a final decision.
"Today's announcement deals with de-powering and de-powering alone," Recht said. "The proposal on disconnection we're continuing to consider. It's a complex issue."
NHTSA said that under the new rules the force with which air bags inflate could be reduced by as much as 35 percent.
"Safety is our highest priority, and we moved at a record pace to devise an interim solution that can be adopted quickly," NHTSA Administrator Ricardo Martinez said in a statment.
While the bags are credited with saving about 1,750 lives since being introduced in the 1980s, their 200-mph (320-kph) inflating force has been blamed for deaths in 62 crashes.

NHTSA said 38 children have died from fatal injuries caused by air bags. Earlier estimates by the agency have shown that if bags on U.S. cars are reduced in power, 643 lives could be saved a year, although up to 2,000 drivers and passengers not wearing seat belts could be killed.
Automakers support the lower-power bags but are vehemently opposed to disconnecting them, which the companies say will claim more lives than they save.
"If we start letting people disconnect air bags willy-nilly, there will be a lot of deaths," Chrysler Corp. spokesman Jason Vines said.
"We commend NHTSA for taking a positive step toward making air bags safer and for saying 'Wait a minute, let's not be reckless about this (disconnection issue.'"

General Motors Corp. also issued a statement applauding NHTSA's action, which sets up new rules for a new test protocol. The new test will allow GM to install de-powered air bags in cars this summer -- about two years earlier than would have been possible under the previous rules, GM said.

However, Recht at NHTSA noted people don't have to wait for new 1998 models to increase their safety -- they can achieve that today by wearing their seat belts and strapping small children into the back seat and not the front.

NHTSA cautioned the new rule was an interim plan to promote safety. Martinez said a long-term solution was still in the works, including technology to adjust air bag deployment to crash severity, size of the occupant and position.
